artists.biography:
Derek and the Dominos were a blues rock band formed in the spring of 1970 by guitarist and singer Eric Clapton with keyboardist Bobby Whitlock, bassist Carl Radle and drummer Jim Gordon, who had all played with Clapton in Delaney, Bonnie & Friends. Duane Allman was also invited by Clapton to join the sessions to add slide guitar to a number of tracks. Allman was then asked to join permanently, but declined.

The band released only one studio album, Layla and Other Assorted Love Songs. The album featured slide guitar from guitarist Duane Allman, who contributed powerful slide guitar work on most of the cuts on the album. His most memorable contribution was to the album's title track, "Layla". The album went on to receive critical acclaim, but initially faltered in sales and in radio airplay. Although released in 1970 it was not until March 1972 that the album's single "Layla" (a tale of unrequited love inspired by Clapton's relationship with his friend George Harrison's wife, Pattie Boyd Harrison) would make the top ten in both the United States and the United Kingdom. The album, which has received praise from both critics and fans alike, is often considered to be the defining achievement of Clapton's career.

perplexity.description:
Layla and Other Assorted Love Songs, released on November 9, 1970, is the only studio album by Derek and the Dominos, an English-American rock band led by Eric Clapton. The album is a seminal work in the rock and blues genres, blending raw emotional intensity with intricate guitar work. It features a mix of original compositions and covers, with standout tracks like the title song "Layla," which is widely regarded as Clapton's greatest musical achievement. The album's sound is deeply rooted in blues rock, highlighted by the interplay between Clapton's guitar and Duane Allman's slide guitar, who contributed to 11 of the 14 tracks, adding a distinctive dual-guitar dynamic that defines the album's style.

In terms of its place in Derek and the Dominos' discography, this album stands alone as their sole studio release, capturing a unique moment in Clapton's career when he sought to express personal turmoil through music. Despite its later acclaim, the album initially met with modest commercial success, peaking at number 16 on the US Billboard Top LPs chart and failing to chart in the UK upon release. Over time, however, it has achieved classic status, with "Layla" becoming a rock anthem and the album itself being inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame. Its influence endures as a benchmark of blues-infused rock and a testament to Clapton's artistry outside his solo and other band projects.
